I.1: Our eternal, transcendent, and all-glorious God, who exists forever as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is by His very nature a communicating being (Gen. 1:3; John 1:1; 17:5; Heb. 3:7). He creates (Gen. 1; Ps. 33:9; 147:18; 148:5; Col. 1:15-17; Heb. 11:3) and also governs (Ps. 29; Lam. 3:37-38; Isa. 46:8-11; Col. 1:15-17; Heb. 1:3) by His words, and He has graciously revealed Himself (Deut. 29:29; 1 Sam. 3:21) to humanity (Gen. 1:26; 2:15-17) in order to have fellowship with us (Acts 17:24-27). He has revealed Himself through creation and providence in ways that are clear to all people, leaving no one without a witness of Himself (Gen. 3:8-9; Ps. 19:1-6; Hos. 2:20; John 10:14-15; Acts 14:17; Rom. 1:19-21). He has also revealed Himself through specific words, so that we might come to a fuller knowledge of His character and will (Ps. 19:7-11) and learn what is necessary for salvation and life (2 Tim. 3:15-17; 2 Pet. 1:3-4). Through the means of human language (Exod. 32:16; Heb. 1:1-2), which is fitting and suitable for communicating with those who bear His image, God has preserved in Holy Scripture the only authoritative and complete revelation for all humanity (Rev. 22:18-19).
I.4: We believe and teach that all Scripture is inspired by God. Each author was moved and directed by the Holy Spirit (while preserving their different personalities and styles) to write the Word of God, so that it was recorded without error in the original writings (2 Pet. 1:20-21; 2 Tim. 3:16). Its inspiration is held to be verbal, inerrant, and infallible, and it is our only authority in matters of faith and practice; its truths are absolute and eternal (Matt. 24:35). The Scriptures are the only standard by which we must measure everything we do, inside and outside the church (Acts 20:32; Heb. 4:12). For this reason we affirm “Sola Scriptura,” as proclaimed by the Reformers.
I.5: We believe and teach that the Bible contains 66 books, 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament, as has been recognized since the early church. Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude, and Revelation.
II.2: There is only one (Deut. 6:4; 1 Cor. 8:4-5) living and true God (Jer. 10:10; John 17:3; 1 Thess. 1:9), who is infinite in His being (Exod. 3:14; Job 11:7-9), power (Ps. 24:8; Matt. 19:26), and perfections (Matt. 5:48). God is eternal (Ps. 90:2; Rev. 1:8), independent, and self-sufficient; He has life in Himself and needs no one and nothing (Ps. 50:10-12; 102:25-27; Acts 17:24-25). He is spirit (John 4:24), transcendent and invisible (Rom. 1:20), without limitation or imperfection (Ps. 18:30), unchanging (Mal. 3:6; James 1:17), and present everywhere in the fullness of His being (Jer. 23:23-24; Ps. 139:7-10). His knowledge is exhaustive, including all things actual and possible, so that nothing—past, present, or future—is hidden from His sight (Isa. 42:8; 1 John 3:20). God is not divided into parts; rather, His whole being includes all His attributes: He is wholly holy (Ps. 99:9; Rev. 15:4), loving (1 John 4:8), wise (Ps. 104:24; Rom. 16:27), just (Deut. 32:4; Rom. 3:25-26), good (Ps. 106:1; Luke 18:19), merciful (Exod. 34:6; 2 Cor. 1:3), full of grace (Ps. 103:8; 1 Pet. 5:10), and true (Ps. 12:6; Prov. 30:5; Titus 1:2). Our God is the infinite source of all that is (Ps. 36:9; John 5:26), who created all things (Gen. 1:1; Ps. 33:6, 9; John 1:3), and all things exist through Him and for Him (Rom. 11:36; Col. 1:16). He is supremely powerful to accomplish all His holy and perfect will, and He rules over His creation with absolute dominion (Ps. 115:3; 66:7), justice (Ps. 9:8; 36:6), wisdom (Ps. 104:24; Rom. 16:27), and love (Exod. 34:6; Ps. 119:64). Because He is transcendent, God is incomprehensible in His being and His works; nevertheless, He reveals Himself in such a way that we can know Him truly and personally (Ps. 145:3; 1 Cor. 2:10-12; Rom. 11:33; Col. 1:10; Jer. 9:23-24).
II.4: The one true God exists eternally as three persons—Father (John 6:27; Titus 1:4), Son (John 1:1; 8:58; Col. 2:9), and Holy Spirit (Heb. 9:14; 1 Cor. 3:16; Acts 5:3-4)—infinitely excellent and all-glorious. Each person is fully God, sharing the same deity, attributes, and essential nature, and yet there is only one God (Deut. 6:4; Isa. 45:21-22). Each person is distinct, yet God is not divided into three parts, natures, or gods by this distinction. The Father has always existed as Father, the unbegotten source of all life (Rom. 11:36; Eph. 4:6). The Son has always existed as Son, eternally begotten of the Father, uncreated and without beginning, of one essence with the Father (John 1:1-4; 10:30; Heb. 1:3, 5). The Holy Spirit has always existed as Spirit, proceeding eternally from the Father and the Son, and of one essence with them (John 15:26; Gal. 4:6). The Godhead thus exists in perfect unity, indivisible in nature and substance, yet as inseparably distinct persons who enjoy a fullness of fellowship and love (John 3:35; 14:31; 17:24).
II.6: God the Father, the first Person of the Trinity, is the all-powerful Ruler and Creator of the universe (Gen. 1:1-31; Ps. 146:6) and is sovereign in both creation and redemption (Rom. 11:36). He does whatever He pleases (Ps. 115:3; 135:6), and no one limits Him. His sovereignty does not cancel human responsibility (1 Pet. 1:17).
II.8: Jesus Christ, God the Son, is co-eternal with God the Father and God the Holy Spirit, and yet eternally begotten of the Father. He possesses all the divine attributes and is co-equal and consubstantial with the Father (John 10:30; 14:9). Jesus secured our redemption by willingly offering His life on the cross. His sacrifice was substitutionary, propitiatory, and redemptive (John 10:15; Rom. 3:24-25; 5:8; 1 Pet. 2:24; 1 John 2:2). After His crucifixion, Jesus rose bodily (not merely spiritually or metaphorically) from the dead, and so demonstrated that He is God in human flesh (Matt. 28; Mark 16; Luke 24; John 20-21; Acts 1; 9; 1 Cor. 15).
II.10: The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Triune God and, like the Son, co-eternal and co-equal with the Father. He is not a “thing” or a “force”; He is a person. He has intellect (1 Cor. 2:9-11), emotions (Eph. 4:30; Rom. 15:30), and will or desire (1 Cor. 12:7-11). He speaks (Acts 8:26-29), commands (John 14:26), teaches, and prays (Rom. 8:26-28). He can be lied to (Acts 5:1-3), blasphemed (Matt. 12:31-32), resisted (Acts 7:51), and insulted (Heb. 10:28-29). All of these are characteristics and qualities of a Person. Although He is not the same Person as God the Father, He is of the same essence and nature. He convicts people of sin, of righteousness, and of the certainty of judgment unless they repent (John 16:7-11). He grants regeneration (John 3:1-5; Titus 3:5-6) and repentance (Acts 5:31; 11:18; 2 Tim. 2:23-25) to the elect. He dwells in every believer (Rom. 8:9; 1 Cor. 6:19-20), intercedes for every believer (Rom. 8:26), and seals every believer for eternity (Eph. 1:13-14).
II.11: c) The Gifts of the Spirit
II.12: Christ loves the church, His body, and provides for its health and growth through the Holy Spirit (John 16:4-15; Eph. 4:7-8, 13-16; 5:25-27). In addition to giving new life, the Spirit sovereignly gives gifts to every believer (1 Cor. 12:7, 11). Spiritual gifts are those abilities and expressions of God’s power given by His grace for the glory of Christ and the building up of the church (1 Cor. 12:7; 14:26; Eph. 4:12). The variety of these gifts—some permanent and others occasional, some more natural and others more extraordinary—reflects (Rom. 12:6-8; 1 Cor. 12:4-11, 28-30; 1 Pet. 4:10-11; Eph. 4:11-12) the diversity of the members of Christ’s body (1 Cor. 12:21-26) and shows our need for one another (1 Cor. 14:1; 13:1-3; 14:33). The gifts are not to be exercised with fear, pride, or disorder, but with faith, love, and order (1 Cor. 13:1-3; 14:1; 14:33), and always in submission to the authority of Scripture as God’s final revelation (1 Thess. 5:19-21; 1 Cor. 14:29; 2 Tim. 3:16; Rev. 22:18-19). All the spiritual gifts remain in operation in the church and are given for the good of the church and for its witness to the world. We should therefore earnestly desire them and practice them until Christ returns (1 Cor. 1:7; 12:31; 13:8-12; 14:1, 12).
III.0: We believe and teach that man was created by God in His image and likeness: “male and female He created them” (Gen. 1:27). Therefore, we understand that the Bible teaches the existence of these two genders only. We believe and teach that because man was created in the image and likeness of God, he is a spiritual, moral, rational, and emotional being with a will of his own. This enables man to relate to God and to others, to discern good and evil, to reason, to experience emotions, and to decide his course of action within the limits God has set. We believe and teach that man is made up of two parts: body and spirit (Gen. 2:7; James 2:26). In many passages of Scripture the words soul and spirit are used interchangeably (1 Cor. 5:5; James 5:20). God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into him the breath of life. For this reason man is called to glorify the Lord with his whole being (1 Cor. 6:20; Rom. 12:1). We believe and teach that man was created as God’s representative on earth, serving as steward over creation (Gen. 1:28-30). We believe and teach that God created man without sin, free to choose between good and evil, but man sinned by his own choice, staining the image of God and enslaving his will to sin (Gen. 3:6; 2 Tim. 2:25-26). Therefore, man is destined for eternal condemnation unless he is redeemed by grace through the work of Jesus Christ and regenerated by the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:6; 8:7; 3:10-12; John 6:44, 65; 15:5; Eph. 2:1-5; Col. 2:13; 1 Cor. 2:14; Titus 3:3-5).
III.2: We believe, affirm, and teach that salvation is the act by which God, through His love, mercy, and grace, sovereignly intervenes by giving His Son to deliver sinful man from His wrath, so that he may afterward enjoy His glory and even become a co-heir with the Son of God. This salvation is given by grace, through faith in Christ, for the glory of God (Eph. 2:8-9; Gal. 2:21; Rom. 9:16; 11:6). Saving faith rests on the redeeming work of Christ alone: “Christ Alone.” We believe that Jesus lived a life of perfect obedience and died in our place as the Lamb of God, and rose as King of Kings and Lord of Lords, obtaining the forgiveness of sins and justification for all who believe in His name (2 Tim. 1:9; 1 Pet. 2:24; 3:18; 1 Cor. 1:30; 15:3; 2 Cor. 5:4; Rom. 3:24-25; 4:25; 5:6; 8:34; 14:9). And although salvation is a divine decision, man is responsible for his actions and will give an account to God for his works (John 3:36; 2 Cor. 5:10; James 1:13-14).
IV.0: The universal church is the true community of God’s people who worship Him, made up of all the elect of all times (Heb. 12:22-23; 2:12; Eph. 5:25; Rev. 21:2). Throughout the history of salvation, God, by His Word and His Spirit, has been calling sinful people out of the whole human race to create a new, redeemed humanity (Gen. 12:1-3; Exod. 6:7; 19:3-6; Deut. 4:10; Eph. 2:11-22; Col. 1:13), whom Christ purchased with His blood (Acts 20:28; Eph. 1:7; 5:25). When the Spirit was given at Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4), God’s people were reconstituted as His new covenant church (Acts 2:42-47), in continuity with the people of God under the old covenant, but now brought to fulfillment by the work of Christ (Jer. 31:31-33; Rom. 11:25; Eph. 1:23; 2:13-22; 3:6; Heb. 8:8-10). All members of God’s people are united in one body (Eph. 4:4-6; 1 Cor. 12:12-27)—with Christ as its supreme, sustaining, and life-giving head (Col. 1:18; 2:19; Eph. 1:22-23; 4:15-16; 5:23)—and set apart as God’s possession and for His purposes (1 Pet. 2:9-10; Lev. 19:2).
IV.2: As an expression of Christ’s universal church, the local church is the focal point of God’s plan to bring His people to maturity and to save sinners (Eph. 3:10; 1 Tim. 3:15; Matt. 28:18-20). Therefore, every Christian should join a specific local church as a committed member (Acts 2:47; 1 Cor. 1:2; 1 Thess. 1:1). A genuine church is marked by the faithful preaching of the Word (2 Tim. 2:15; 4:1-2; Titus 1:9), the right administration of the sacraments (Matt. 28:19; Acts 2:38; Rom. 6:3-4; Matt. 26:26-28; 1 Cor. 11:17-34), and the proper exercise of church discipline (Matt. 18:15-17; 1 Cor. 5:1-13). Even genuine churches are imperfect: a variety of unbelievers are often found hidden among the true flock (2 Tim. 2:16-19; Acts 20:29-30; 2 Tim. 4:10), and they are vulnerable to theological error and moral failure (1 Cor. 3:1-3; 5:1; 1 Tim. 5:20; 2 Tim. 4:3-4; Rev. 2:5, 14-16, 20-23; 3:2-3, 15-19). Nevertheless, Christ is steadfast in His commitment to build His church, and He will surely bring it to maturity (Matt. 16:18; Eph. 5:25-27; Rev. 19:7-9).
V.0: We believe, affirm, and teach that the Church has received from the Lord Jesus two ordinances that serve as signs of the Covenant of Grace (Matt. 28:19; 1 Cor. 11:23). These are the Lord’s Supper and Baptism.
V.2: The Lord’s Supper was instituted by Jesus the night before He was crucified (Matt. 26:26-30), to be celebrated regularly by believers baptized by immersion, with a frequency determined by each local church, as a remembrance of what He would do for us the next day at Calvary (Luke 22:19-20; 1 Cor. 11:26). We believe that the elements shared, the bread and the wine, symbolize the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 11:26-28; Matt. 26:29). In celebrating this remembrance we follow the guidelines given in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26.
V.4: Baptism is to be done by immersion, after a person has believed in Christ as Lord and Savior. We do it as a picture of our union with Him: dying to sin and rising to new life. Every believer should be baptized willingly, as a public testimony of their faith and not as a means of salvation (Matt. 28:19; Eph. 2:8-9).
VI.0: As the body of Christ, the church exists to worship God (Col. 3:16; Eph. 5:18-20), to build up His people and bring them to maturity (Eph. 4:12-13; Col. 1:28), and to bear witness to Christ and His kingdom throughout the world (Matt. 28:19). Governed by Scripture, the church gathers for the teaching of the Word (2 Tim. 4:1-2; 1 Tim. 4:13; Eph. 4:11-12), prayer (Acts 2:42; 1 Tim. 2:1-2), the sacraments (Rom. 6:3-4; 1 Cor. 11:17-34), congregational singing (Col. 3:16; Eph. 5:18-20), fellowship, and mutual edification through the exercise of spiritual gifts (1 Cor. 12:7; 14:26; 1 Thess. 5:11; 1 Pet. 4:10). Just as the Father sent Jesus into the world, so Jesus has sent His people into the world in the power of the Spirit (John 17:18; 20:21; Luke 24:44-49; Acts 1:5-8). The mission of the church is to make disciples of all nations, teaching them to observe everything Christ has commanded (Matt. 28:18-20). We do this by proclaiming His gospel, planting churches, and adorning the proclamation of the gospel with our love and good works. There will always be an assembly of believers on earth, because the Lord promises to build, guide, and preserve His church until the end of the world (Matt. 16:18). When Christ returns, He will gather and perfect His church, from every tribe, tongue, and nation, as a people for His own possession, and He will dwell with them forever (1 Thess. 4:16-17; 1 John 3:2; 1 Cor. 15:51-52; 2 Cor. 5:1; Titus 2:13-14; Rev. 7:13-17; 19:6-9; 21:1-4).
VII.0: We believe and teach that the return of Christ will be personal, sudden, visible, and bodily (Matt. 24:44; Acts 1:11; 1 Thess. 4:16; 5:1-10; Heb. 9:28; Rev. 22:7, 12, 20).
VII.1: No one knows the day or the hour of our Lord’s coming (Matt. 24:44; 25:1-13). The believer should await Christ’s return with expectation, joy, and eagerness (Rev. 22:20; Titus 2:12-13; 1 Cor. 16:22). We believe and teach that there will be a great tribulation (Mark 13:7-8, 19-20; Matt. 24:15, 21; Luke 21:20-24; Dan. 12:1), in which we will see false prophets arise (Matt. 24:23-24). There will be signs in the heavens (Matt. 24:29-30), the rise of a great apostasy (2 Tim. 3:1-5; Matt. 24:5, 11), and the appearance of the Antichrist (2 Thess. 2:1-10). All of this is only the beginning of birth pains (Matt. 24:3-9). We believe and teach that the Church will be raptured to meet the Lord in the clouds (1 Thess. 4:13-18; 1 Cor. 15:51-54). We believe and teach that there will be a thousand-year reign (Rev. 20:1-6; Isa. 11:6-11; 65:20), during which Satan will be bound; after this time he will be released and will gather multitudes of unbelievers to make war against the Lord (Rev. 20:7-9). In this final battle Satan will be defeated forever and thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet will also be, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever (Rev. 20:10). (We note that the chronology of these events is still debated, even among the best scholars.)
VIII.0: God has ordained the family as the foundational institution of human society. It is made up of persons related to one another by marriage, blood, or adoption. Marriage is the union of one man and one woman only, in a covenant commitment for life. It is God’s unique gift to reveal the union between Christ and His church, and to give the man and the woman in marriage the framework for intimate companionship, the channel of sexual expression according to biblical standards, and the means for the procreation of the human race. The husband and wife are of equal worth before God, since both are created in God’s image. The marriage relationship models the way God relates to His people. A husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church. He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, protect, and lead his family. A wife is to submit graciously to the servant leadership of her husband, even as the church willingly submits to the headship of Christ. She, being in the image of God as is her husband and thus equal to him, has the God-given responsibility to respect her husband and to serve as his helper in managing the household and nurturing the next generation. Children, from the moment of conception, are a blessing and heritage from the Lord. Parents are to demonstrate to their children God’s pattern for marriage. Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through a consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth. Children are to honor and obey their parents.
